"Here are research options from several root questions, one per line as key: title. summary, where a key looks like R2:physical:W4. Group options that ask the same question of the same kind of system; every key goes in exactly one cluster, and a key that matches nothing is its own cluster. Name each cluster's topic in at least three words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
R1:physical:K1: Single-chain MCMC mixing: the sequential autocorrelation bottleneck. A single Markov chain for a lumped conceptual model must run many serial iterations because posterior samples are autocorrelated; each step conditions on the previous state, and more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate.
R1:physical:K2: Ensemble / differential-evolution MCMC: running many chains in parallel. DREAM-style samplers run N chains simultaneously, generating each chain's proposal from differences of other chains' states; this improves exploration of multimodal/correlated hydrologic posteriors and enables Gelman–Rubin cross-chain diagnostics, and it is the one place where more GPUs change what gets sampled (by raising chain count) without lowering per-chain autocorrelation.
R1:physical:K3: Expensive distributed / high-dimensional forward models (MT-DREAM(ZS), MGB, SWAT). For spatially distributed models with hundreds-to-thousands of parameters the forward-model cost dominates the calibration budget, and the workload decomposes into thousands of independent model runs that are embarrassingly parallel across chains and parameter sets; here compute is a genuinely binding constraint that parallelism relieves.
R1:physical:K4: Large-sample multi-catchment calibration (CAMELS). Calibrating many catchments (CAMELS provides 671 US catchments) is embarrassingly parallel because each catchment is independently calibratable, so GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments get a proper Bayesian treatment rather than point optimization.
R1:interp:K1: Train sparse autoencoders on LSTM rainfall-runoff internals to expose representation-level equifinality. Apply Goodfire-style sparse autoencoders to LSTM cell-state activations to recover a sparse dictionary of hydrological features, then ask which features are uniquely constrained by the runoff record and which interchangeable feature sets reproduce it, reframing the framer's equifinality as non-identifiability of internal features.
R1:interp:K2: Steer SAE features of a differentiable rainfall-runoff model to separate identifiable from equifinal directions. Use Goodfire-style feature steering on a differentiable RR model (LSTM or autodiff GR4J) to measure which features causally change the simulated runoff and which do not, producing an intervention-based map of the posterior geometry that sets the autocorrelation time.
R1:interp:K3: Reparameterize the calibration with active subspaces to shorten the MCMC chain. Identify the few data-informed directions along which the forward model varies (the active subspace) and run MCMC only on those while sampling the prior elsewhere, the non-neural, interpretability-flavored cousin of feature extraction that directly attacks the autocorrelation time through reparameterization rather than hardware.
